title: The Feast of the Unawakened Heir
summary: A dynastic killing, an unconscious sovereign, and a mountain crossing expose the dependence of royal power upon coerced households and uncertain histories.
source_notes: A long reign supported by a personally dependent army and extensive dynastic offspring becomes a fortress monarchy tied to coercive household pledges.
Historical drama, satire, and unsettling family stories become conflicting succession plays whose performance changes with patronage.

A private royal killing and the brief reign of an unconscious heir become an unresolved succession interruption, without reproducing modern weapons or assigning an invented explanation to the real event.
A famous mountain crossing with uncertain routes becomes an expedition reconstructed through animal losses and contradictory place names.

entries.title: Hevren of the Many Courtyards
entries.body:
Hevren allocated a courtyard to each recognized branch of his household, then charged their residents for its maintenance. His long peace depended on continual fortress labor. Descendants invoke his protection while disagreeing about whether workers were ever entitled to leave.

Later accounts make Hevren of the Many Courtyards the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Feast of the Unawakened Heir. For fifty-three years, King Hevren expanded mountain fortresses using labor bound through inherited household pledges. His numerous descendants occupied competing commands. At a private feast in 667, nine senior relatives died and an injured heir was proclaimed sovereign without awakening. A surviving uncle ordered a winter crossing to secure the southern granaries before rival claimants could respond. Pack herds suffered terribly and the army reached its objective unable to carry food home. A satirist later composed three contradictory succession plays. Court readers preserve only the version flattering their patron; caravan households preserve the versions in which servants, animals, and weather determine the outcome.

In the connected record, [The Closed Feast Hall](b006-the-closed-feast-hall.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Sleeping Hand Limit](b006-the-sleeping-hand-limit.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether the crown’s descendants can release coerced labor claims without first agreeing which predecessor possessed the authority to make them.

entries.title: The Closed Feast Hall
entries.body:
The hall retains nine patched places where floor tiles were lifted for investigation. Later restorers arranged them symmetrically, creating a misleading impression of an orderly scene. Servants’ statements describe confusion, blocked doors, and an injured heir carried through the kitchen.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Hearthbound Guard
entries.body:
Guard households received grain in exchange for sons’ service and daughters’ provisioning work. The crown calls their loyalty voluntary. Ancestral tallies bind only specific winter deliveries, leaving the broader prohibition on departure dependent upon living officers and threats to relatives.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Reign of Three Sleeps
entries.body:
The wounded heir ruled for three nights without speaking. Officials authenticated orders by placing his hand near a water bowl. Competing witnesses disagree about whether his fingers moved, making the distinction between bodily presence and consent politically consequential.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Unlifted Feast Cup
entries.body:
The heir’s cup contains residue inconsistent with its ceremonial wine. That establishes reuse, not poisoning. A court faction wants the cup destroyed to end speculation; kitchen custodians preserve it beside the serving schedule, which explains several ordinary reasons for its contents.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Third Night Listening
entries.body:
Families sit beside a sleeping relative on the succession anniversary and refrain from answering questions for them. Some transform the custom into divination. Its earliest account is a servant’s protest against ministers treating silence as convenient approval.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Three Hevren Plays
entries.body:
Each play assigns the same succession to a different cause: inheritance, provisioning, or fear. Their shared comic servant changes patrons between scenes. Authorities call the versions contradictory; performers consider that contradiction the work’s central account of political dependence.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Broadfoot Snow Ox
entries.body:
Broadfoot oxen cross crusted snow but overheat on sheltered descents. Officers ordered them kept in heavy covers for a royal display, killing more animals than the storm did. Herdsmen’s descendants still remove ornamental coverings before entering the lower pass.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Uncertain King’s Crossing
entries.body:
Three valleys claim the expedition’s route from similar place names. Animal bone deposits support passage through two but cannot establish direction. Guides sell competing commemorative journeys, while scholars warn that no honest reconstruction can settle every stage.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Sleeping Hand Limit
entries.body:
A hand touching water cannot authenticate an undertaking unless a witness establishes conscious assent. The ruling threatens old royal contracts. Creditors seek exceptions for sovereigns, claiming ordinary limits would make succession too precarious to finance.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Southern Granary Arrival
entries.body:
The crossing army seized a granary then lacked sound animals to transport its grain. Commanders declared victory and remained through winter. Local households paid the occupation’s food costs, illustrating how a famous feat could fail the purpose that justified it.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Satirist’s Double Mask
entries.body:
One face depicts a ruler; the reverse depicts a storekeeper. Actors turn it without changing the speech, shifting its apparent authority. The original mask’s repairs show repeated use by small troupes rather than the court festival that now claims exclusive custody.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Uncovered Descent
entries.body:
Caravan crews uncover pack animals before leaving the snow shelf, regardless of visiting dignitaries’ expectations. A ritual song explains the old loss. Young keepers teach the physiological reason alongside the song so memory remains useful when ceremonial details change.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Bone and Place Ledger
entries.body:
The ledger compares route names with animal remains and feeding needs. It leaves several stretches unresolved. Its refusal to produce a complete royal itinerary has reduced donations but saved guides from repeating dangerous journeys justified by attractive historical speculation.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Feast Hall Condensation
entries.body:
Nine patches darken during crowded meals because the repaired floor conducts moisture differently. One patch darkens when the hall is empty. Investigators record both patterns, resisting the choice between dismissing every report and declaring every damp tile a murdered relative’s speech.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Fortress Lime Carrying
entries.body:
Workers carry lime uphill in sealed skins, then return with grain rather than empty loads. Royal contracts require both trips but pay for one. Their petition uses actual burden measurements to expose how a ceremonial labor pledge became continual extraction.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Unrecognized Children’s Release
entries.body:
Unrecognized descendants offer to surrender disputed royal claims in exchange for ending guard bondage. Established branches object that this acknowledges their standing. Workers insist the release cannot depend on preserving the same genealogy that erased half its witnesses.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
